title: Orthopedic Implants Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2033
executive_summary:
Published estimates of the orthopedic implants market put its 2025 or 2026 base between $28.45 billion and $61.61 billion -- a 2.17x spread. The published growth rates run only from 3.97% to 5.8%, a 1.46x spread. Nobody really disagrees about how fast this market grows. They disagree about what is in it.

This is the best-disclosed market we have examined, and that makes the disagreement settleable. Five companies disclose orthopaedic segment revenue outright: Stryker's Orthopaedics segment at $9,469 million for 2025, Zimmer Biomet's whole company at $8,232 million, Johnson & Johnson's Orthopaedics franchise at $9,258 million, Smith+Nephew's Orthopaedics segment at $2,437 million, and Medtronic's Cranial & Spinal Technologies division at $4,973 million for a fiscal year ended April 2025. Those five sum to $34,369 million.

That sum is 120.8% of 360iResearch's entire published global market of $28.45 billion -- five companies disclosing 21% more revenue than the whole market is said to contain. Zimmer Biomet alone, an orthopaedics pure-play whose revenue is therefore a hard floor on any definition including knees and hips, is 28.9% of it; Zimmer Biomet plus Stryker Orthopaedics is 62.2%. Neither is possible in an industry that also contains Globus Medical, Arthrex, Medacta, B.Braun Aesculap, Enovis and the whole Chinese domestic supply base.

Against Persistence Market Research's $48.4 billion for 2026 the same five disclosures are 71.0% -- high, but plausible for an industry whose top five are known to dominate it. A second test confirms the order of magnitude: the four reconstructive players disclose $14,850 million of knee and hip implant revenue, which against OECD-implied hip and knee replacement volume is about $3,040 per procedure, inside the measured per-case implant cost range. We publish $48.4 billion for 2026 rising to $70.9 billion by 2033 at 5.6%, and name the three scope decisions that move the number.
market_context:
The word that moves this market's size is not implant, it is skeletal. Three product families sit inside or outside a published figure depending on the analyst, and each is worth billions.

Spinal implants are the first. Persistence names them as a product type; a reconstructive-only reading excludes them. Medtronic alone disclosed $4,973 million of Cranial & Spinal Technologies revenue for its fiscal 2025, more than a sixth of the narrowest published global market on its own. Stryker, by contrast, reported Spinal Implants of just $185 million within a $9,469 million Orthopaedics segment, having divested its US spinal implants business -- so a reader who treats Stryker's orthopaedic revenue as covering spine is reading the wrong company.

Trauma fixation and craniomaxillofacial implants are the second. They are the largest single line in two of the five big disclosures: Stryker's Trauma and Extremities was $3,948 million in 2025 and J&J's Trauma was $3,146 million -- each larger than either company's knee or hip business.

Dental implants are the third. No source in our set states whether dental is in or out, except Persistence by omission. It is the most common silent inclusion in any category called implants, and it is the first question to ask of any figure quoted in this market.
forecast_analysis:
The headline comes from Persistence Market Research, read from the publisher's own page on 16 October 2026: $48.4 billion for 2026, $70.9 billion for 2033, a 5.6% CAGR for 2026-2033, against a published historical $37.3 billion for 2020 at a 4.4% historical rate. Both endpoints are the publisher's own published figures rather than derivations, which is unusual, and the arithmetic closes: 48.4 x 1.056^7 = 70.88 against the published 70.9, an implied 5.61% against a stated 5.6%. The intermediate years shown here are interpolation at that rate, not separately sourced observations.

It was chosen because it is the only source in the set we could read directly from the publisher's own page -- every competing figure came through a search summary, one publisher page returned HTTP 403, and one attribution could not be verified at all -- and because it is the only one with a fully stated product scope naming reconstructive joints, spinal implants, trauma fixation and CMF. That is precisely the decision that moves this market's base by 2.17x.

It is also the series the disclosed record supports. At $48.4 billion, five disclosed segment revenue lines are 71.0% of the market; at $28.45 billion they are 120.8% of it. Readers should treat a published growth rate here as the stable part of the literature and a published base as a scope statement.

market_overview.summary: On the broad definition we adopt -- reconstructive joint replacement, spinal implants, trauma fixation and craniomaxillofacial implants, excluding dental -- the orthopedic implants market is $48.4 billion in 2026, projected to $70.9 billion by 2033 at a 5.6% CAGR. A narrower reading published by 360iResearch puts 2025 at $28.45 billion, but five companies disclose $34.37 billion of orthopaedic segment revenue between them, exceeding that whole market by 21%, and two of them alone are 62.2% of it. The spread across published bases is 2.17x; across published growth rates it is only 1.46x.
key_trends: Published base-year estimates spread 2.17x ($28.45B to $61.61B) while published CAGRs spread only 1.46x (3.97% to 5.8%)
Five disclosed orthopaedic revenue lines sum to $34.37B, which is 120.8% of the narrowest published global market and 71.0% of the broadest
Trauma and extremities is now larger than knees or hips at both Stryker ($3,948M) and J&J ($3,146M), reversing the usual mental model of this market
Disclosed knee and hip implant revenue works out at about $3,040 per OECD hip or knee replacement, inside the measured per-case implant cost range
OECD hip and knee replacement rates rose from 172 and 119 per 100,000 in 2021 to 198 and 156 in 2023, so procedure volume is growing faster than the published revenue CAGRs
Portfolio reshaping is accelerating: J&J plans to spin off orthopaedics within 18 to 24 months, Stryker has exited US spinal implants, and Zimmer Biomet bought Paragon 28
market_overview.adoption_level: Standard of care; growth comes from volume and mix rather than from new adoption

drivers: Rising procedure rates in the register: OECD hip replacements went from 172 to 198 per 100,000 and knees from 119 to 156 between the 2021 and 2023 data years
Ageing populations in the high-rate OECD countries, where Germany already performs about 351 hip replacements per 100,000
Migration of joint replacement into ambulatory surgical centres, which Persistence names as the growing end-user channel
Robotic and enabling-technology platforms pulling implant volume through: J&J credits VELYS pull-through for knee growth and Medtronic credits the AiBLE ecosystem for spine
Extremities and trauma, where Zimmer Biomet's S.E.T. line grew 15.2% in 2025 with 10.5 points of that from the Paragon 28 acquisition
restraints: Price deflation: Stryker reported 0.1% lower prices across Orthopaedics in 2025 even while unit volume grew 9.6% in constant currency
China volume-based procurement, which J&J cites as a pressure on every orthopaedics platform; no sourced percentage is available for the price cuts
Core joint growth is low single digit at every disclosing company -- Zimmer Biomet's knees and hips each grew 4.7% reported and Smith+Nephew's each 3.5%
Hospital purchasing concentration, with one study finding 61.0% of per-case implant cost variation attributable to hospital characteristics rather than patients
Reimbursement bundling, which makes the implant a cost line inside a fixed episode payment rather than a revenue line
opportunities: Non-OECD volume, almost entirely outside the procedure rates on which this market's scale is usually reasoned
Revision arthroplasty, which registries track separately and which carries higher implant content per case
Spine enabling technology, where Medtronic's CST division grew 5% on navigation and robotics attachment rather than on implant price
Foot and ankle and other extremities, the only segment growing at double digits in the disclosed record
Consolidation of the mid-cap field -- Globus/NuVasive, Orthofix/SeaSpine, Zimmer Biomet/Paragon 28 -- which is where the market share outside the top five sits
challenges: No vendor share is disclosed by any of the five companies that disclose revenue, so concentration cannot be measured, only bounded
Published market sizes differ by scope rather than measurement, making them unusable for planning without first establishing whether spine, trauma and dental are in
Stryker's exit from US spinal implants and J&J's planned orthopaedics spin-off mean the comparable set of disclosures will change again within two years
Procedure counts are not publicly registered at national level: registries capture a partial sample and OECD figures are rates, not counts

Knees were $3,322.3 million and Hips $2,093.5 million, each up 4.7% reported, and S.E.T. was $2.15 billion, up 15.2% with 10.5 points of that from the Paragon 28 acquisition. Growth is attributed to the AiBLE spine implant and enabling-technology ecosystem, with gains in Core Spine, Biologics and Neurosurgery. Whether this revenue is inside or outside a quoted orthopedic implants figure is the single largest scope question in the category.

Robotics consumables were reclassified into the knee and hip lines so prior years are restated. A trade source reports a $4.15 billion orthopaedic figure for the same company that additionally includes Sports Medicine and Enabling Technology and is not comparable with the segment line.

China volume-based procurement and an orthopaedics restructuring were cited as pressures on every platform.

Reported 2025 net sales of $8.232 billion, up 7.2% reported but 3.9% organic constant currency, with S.E.T. revenue up 15.2% of which 10.5 percentage points came from the Paragon 28 foot and ankle acquisition, and guided 2026 revenue growth of 2.5% to 4.5%.

Published the twelfth American Joint Replacement Registry Annual Report, analysing 4,434,668 validated hip and knee arthroplasty procedures collected from 2012 through 2024 across all 50 states, up 20% from 3,715,320 in the prior edition, from over 5,000 surgeons and 1,200 institutions.

regulatory_landscape: FDA device classification for orthopaedic devices under 21 CFR Part 888, under which most hip and knee prostheses clear by 510(k) as Class II while certain implants require premarket approval
EU Medical Device Regulation 2017/745, which classifies total joint replacement implants as Class III and requires clinical evaluation and post-market clinical follow-up for each

CMS removal of total knee arthroplasty (2018) and total hip arthroplasty (2020) from the Medicare inpatient-only list, which opened outpatient and ambulatory surgical centre settings to these procedures
CMS bundled payment models for lower-extremity joint replacement, which place the implant inside a fixed episode payment and transfer price risk to the provider
China's centralised volume-based procurement for orthopaedic implants, cited by Johnson & Johnson as a pressure on every orthopaedics platform
National arthroplasty registry reporting, including the American Joint Replacement Registry and equivalent national registries, which conditions post-market surveillance evidence for implant systems

primary_research: No primary interviews were conducted for this edition. This report is a synthesis of SEC and 20-F filings, the OECD health statistics, a national arthroplasty registry report and published third-party estimates, and is labelled as such rather than implying fieldwork that did not occur.

research_methodology.data_validation: Market size is taken from published third-party estimates, attributed by name, and presented as published estimates rather than verified measurements. Two grounding tests were run. First, five disclosed orthopaedic revenue lines for 2025 were summed -- Stryker $9,469M, Zimmer Biomet $8,232M, Johnson & Johnson $9,258M, Smith+Nephew $2,437M and Medtronic Cranial & Spinal Technologies $4,973M, totalling $34,369M -- and divided by each publisher's base-year total, giving 71.0% of Persistence's $48.4 billion and 120.8% of 360iResearch's $28.45 billion. Zimmer Biomet alone is 28.9% of the latter and Zimmer Biomet plus Stryker Orthopaedics 62.2%. Second, the four reconstructive players' disclosed knee and hip implant revenue of $14,850M was divided by hip and knee replacement volume implied by OECD rates of 198 and 156 per 100,000 against the OECD population, giving roughly $3,040 per procedure against a measured per-case implant cost range of $1,797 to $12,093. These tests establish that the narrowest published series cannot be the whole market and that the broad reading is in the right order of magnitude. They do not establish the correct market size for either scope. Medtronic's fiscal year ends in April and is not coterminous with the other four; Zimmer Biomet's figure is whole-company revenue, not an implant-only line; the OECD population multiplier is our own sum of member populations against an average that is probably unweighted, so the procedure figure is an estimate rather than a count; the per-case implant cost comparator is from 2008 and US-only; and dividing company revenue by a third party's market total compares differently constructed numbers. No vendor market share is published because none is disclosed, and no regional or country split is published because no named source gives a numeric share of the global total.

faqs.question: How big is the orthopedic implants market?
faqs.answer: On the broad definition we adopt -- reconstructive joints, spinal implants, trauma fixation and craniomaxillofacial implants -- $48.4 billion in 2026, projected to $70.9 billion by 2033 at 5.6%, per Persistence Market Research's published series. Narrower readings put 2025 as low as $28.45 billion, but five companies disclose $34.37 billion of orthopaedic revenue between them, so the narrow figure cannot be the whole market.

faqs.question: Why do published estimates differ by 2.17x?
faqs.answer: Three scope decisions, each worth billions. Whether spinal implants are in: Medtronic alone discloses $4,973 million of them. Whether trauma and craniomaxillofacial are in: those lines are $3,948 million at Stryker and $3,146 million at J&J, each larger than either company's knee business. And whether dental implants are in, which no source in our set states either way.

faqs.question: How can you tell which published figure is wrong?
faqs.answer: By summing the disclosures. Stryker $9,469M, Zimmer Biomet $8,232M, J&J $9,258M, Smith+Nephew $2,437M and Medtronic's spine division $4,973M total $34,369M for 2025. That is 120.8% of 360iResearch's entire $28.45 billion global market. Zimmer Biomet and Stryker Orthopaedics alone are 62.2% of it, which leaves no room for Globus Medical, Arthrex, Medacta, Enovis or the Chinese suppliers.

faqs.question: What does an implant actually cost per operation?
faqs.answer: The four reconstructive players disclose $14,850 million of knee and hip implant revenue. Against hip and knee replacement volume implied by the OECD's rates of 198 and 156 procedures per 100,000 population, that is about $3,040 of manufacturer revenue per procedure. A study of 10,155 total knee replacements at 61 US hospitals found average implant cost per case ranging from $1,797 to $12,093, so $3,040 at the factory gate sits where it should, below hospital acquisition cost.

faqs.question: Who leads the orthopedic implants market?
faqs.answer: On disclosed revenue, Stryker's Orthopaedics segment ($9,469M) and J&J's Orthopaedics franchise ($9,258M) are the largest, with Zimmer Biomet ($8,232M) close behind as the only pure-play. None of the five discloses a market share, and no filing contains one. Any share percentage you are shown in this category is somebody's estimate.

faqs.question: Is procedure volume growing faster than revenue?
faqs.answer: The register says the rates are rising quickly. OECD hip replacements went from 172 per 100,000 in the 2021 data year to 198 in 2023, and knees from 119 to 156. Yet every disclosing company reports low-single-digit growth in core joints, and Stryker reported 0.1% lower prices across Orthopaedics in 2025 on 9.6% constant-currency unit volume growth. Volume growth in this market is partly absorbed by price.

faqs.question: Why does this report show no regional breakdown?
faqs.answer: Because no publisher in the set gives a numeric regional share of the global total. Persistence covers North America, Europe and Asia Pacific and publishes an 8.9% Asia Pacific growth rate, but a growth rate is not a share. The OECD country figures we use -- about 351 hip replacements per 100,000 in Germany, about 349 in Switzerland -- are procedure rates, not market splits, and are used as such.

key_highlights: Published base-year estimates spread 2.17x ($28.45B to $61.61B) while published CAGRs spread only 1.46x (3.97% to 5.8%)
Five disclosed orthopaedic revenue lines sum to $34.37B for 2025 -- 120.8% of the narrowest published global market and 71.0% of the broadest
Zimmer Biomet, an orthopaedics pure-play, is 28.9% of the narrow market on its own; with Stryker Orthopaedics the two are 62.2% of it
Disclosed knee and hip implant revenue of $14,850M is about $3,040 per OECD hip or knee replacement, inside a measured $1,797-$12,093 per-case implant cost range
Trauma and extremities now exceeds knees at both Stryker ($3,948M) and J&J ($3,146M)
Stryker's Spinal Implants line is only $185M of a $9,469M Orthopaedics segment after divesting its US spine business, while Medtronic's spine division alone is $4,973M
OECD hip and knee replacement rates rose from 172 and 119 per 100,000 in 2021 to 198 and 156 in 2023
reader_takeaways: Before quoting an orthopedic implants market size, establish whether spine, trauma, CMF and dental are inside it -- those four decisions move the base by 2.17x
Treat any figure near $28 billion as reconstructive joints at most: five companies disclose 21% more revenue than that whole market is said to contain
Use Zimmer Biomet's whole-company revenue as a floor test on any definition that includes knees and hips, because that is effectively all the company does
Trauma and extremities, not joints, is the largest orthopaedic line at two of the three biggest players -- plan against the disclosed mix, not the mental model
Procedure rates are growing faster than revenue, so model price deflation explicitly rather than assuming volume converts to revenue one for one
